messages.subject: estmating densities at different levels
parts:
Dear List,

I gathered point transect data on different songbird species in different=
=20
forest fragments (strata) in 2 seasons during 3 years.
My main aim is to compare relative densities per species in these=20
fragments. I=92m not interested in comparing densities between species, o=
nly=20
within species between fragments. Therefore, I analyse my data separately=
=20
per species. However, I still have some basic questions and doubts and I=20=

hope you can help me with answering them.

First, I analysed densities by pooling all data per species (over years=20=

and seasons), stratifying per forest fragment (detection function=20
estimated per stratum, (1)). The histograms for some fragments revealed=20=

that another bin grouping and truncation distance would give a better fit=
.=20
Therefore, I decided to do the analyses also seperately per fragment (and=
,=20
of course, per species), making an individual decision for truncation and=
=20
grouping for each fragment and selecting the best model for each bird=20
species per fragment. I did this to test if the model, used for pooled=20=

data in the stratified analysis (see (1)), was robust. Densities estimate=
d=20
with pooled data (detection function per stratum) were very similar to th=
e=20
densities estimated when separate analyses per species/fragment were run,=
=20
except for those fragments where sample size was low (< 50 observations).=
=20
My feeling is that it is then more logic to keep to the pooled data=20
stratified per fragment. Is this correct? Or should I choose 1 model,=20
based on the smallest summed AIC=92s (sum of AIC values of all fragments =
for=20
that species per model and then choose lowest sum; as I could find as=20
suggestion by Steven in his reply to the mail of Kristin A Bratland on=20=

25/10/2006)?

One model (based on the pooled data) had a lower AIC value but proved to=20=

be less robust (when comparing density estimates from pooled data versus=20=

the individual fragment-approach). Therefore, I intend to choose the=20
second model or do a bootstrap analysis. I wonder if a bootstrap analysis=
=20
is possible with MCDS and stratification (I would enter season, as well a=
s=20
weather-related parameters, as covariables and stratify per forest=20
fragment)?

If I want to compare the densities for one species between fragments per=20=

year, do I need to use a nested design? But the problem then is that the=20=

sample size per species per year is not large enough. I could stratify pe=
r=20
year and use fragment as a covariable instead of stratifying per fragment=
,=20
but this would mean I wouldn=92t get standard errors for the fragment =96=
=20
level. So is there no solution to get density estimates and errors per=20=

species, fragment and year, other than doing a separate analysis per=20
species- fragment combination and stratifying per year? Even if this=20
separate analysis would be a solution, this would only be possible for=20=

those species that are abundant enough to estimate detection functions pe=
r=20
fragment.

A last question: Can I simply estimate densities per feeding guild (eg=20=

frugivores, insectivores) by hand by adding the densities of the species=20=

belonging to the same guild and calculating the variance?


Thanks a lot for your help!

Val=E9rie Lehouck
